summary:
Luna Crew is a browser game for children aged 7–12 that turns managing a lunar base into an interactive learning experience. Players divide ten work points between power, life support, shielding and science. The three survival systems support the crew, while science earns Mission Points. Players preview their plans, observe resource changes and adjust their strategy.

Our game addresses the challenge by helping children experience the decisions astronauts face when resources and time are limited. We use NASA DONKI solar flare records to inform storm scenarios, RadLab’s ISS radiation readings as scientific reference, and OSD-476 research on plants grown in Apollo lunar soil for science quizzes. Resource changes and storm damage follow simplified educational game rules.

Our goal is to help children move beyond memorizing space facts to understanding how mission systems depend on one another. Producing oxygen and growing food also require electricity. Through these choices, children can practise planning, explain resource trade-offs and develop a greater appreciation of the air, water and protection Earth provides.
details:
Luna Crew: Moon Base Mission is an educational browser game designed for children aged 7–12. Players become the Mission Planner of a lunar base, working alongside Commander Nova, Dr. Sprout and Pip, a helper rover. The game addresses the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge by turning the requirements of space exploration into decisions children can make and understand.

Each round, players divide ten work points between Power, Life Support, Shield and Science. These jobs have different effects and priorities. In our simplified game model, Power work provides five Power units per point during daytime and one at night. Life Support work provides four units per point while consuming electricity. Shield work adds four protection units per point, while Science earns ten Mission Points without replenishing survival resources. Players must therefore balance crew safety with scientific progress.

The systems also interact. Greenhouse lights support food production but consume electricity. During a storm, players can shelter or continue working. Sheltering protects the crew but pauses jobs while essential systems continue consuming resources. Before pressing GO, players can preview expected resource changes. Afterwards, a breakdown explains how their jobs, lighting choices, resource consumption and events produced the result.

A progressive mission map introduces these ideas through lessons such as First Light, The Long Night, Ice Rescue, Storm Watch and Moon Garden. A longer Full Mission combines them, while Mission of the Day and Challenge Mode provide further opportunities to practise. Science quizzes, a journal, stars and badges reinforce learning and encourage replay.

We use three main NASA data sources:

  • DONKI: Saved solar flare and solar energetic particle event records provide event dates, flare classes and source links. Flare classes and particle-event associations feed our team-designed storm difficulty system, affecting the shielding needed to continue working. This is an educational mapping, rather than a calculation of radiation exposure on the Moon. DONKI provides the underlying space-weather records and event relationships.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository, OSD-476: Findings from an Earth-based experiment using Apollo lunar soil support our greenhouse explanations and science questions. The study showed that plants could grow in returned lunar material, but developed slowly and showed stress.
  • RadLab: A saved DosTel1 radiation reading from the International Space Station appears on the storm screen as scientific reference. Its observation location, date and unit distinguish it from the lunar scenario and the selected storm. RadLab provides access to radiation measurements from multiple instruments and spacecraft.

NASA reference pages on lunar ice, oxygen production, water recycling, plant growth and radiation protection support additional dialogue and quizzes. The Canadian Space Agency’s food-production toolkit provides complementary educational material. The game uses saved data files, with a scheduled daily DONKI update, an archive fallback and a labelled fictional training alert when usable records are unavailable.

We developed the game using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG graphics and animation, JSON content files, and the Web Audio API for sound and music. Node.js scripts retrieve NASA data, GitHub Actions supports data updates and deployment, and GitHub Pages hosts the game. Progress is saved locally in the browser. Cursor and Claude assisted with code, artwork, animation, audio and Japanese text, with our team reviewing the rules and scientific content. No specialised hardware is required.

Our creative approach combines character-driven storytelling, connected resource decisions and source-linked science. Children encounter scientific information when it becomes relevant to a choice. We considered reading load, accessibility, game balance, scientific accuracy and classroom use. English and Japanese support, adjustable text size, high contrast, reduced motion and optional sound help make the experience accessible.

Our intended impact is to help children explain at least one real mission trade-off in their own words—for example, why producing oxygen also requires electricity. Through prediction, feedback and repeated attempts, we aim to develop planning and problem-solving skills while encouraging appreciation of the air, water and protection Earth provides.
